title: Detached buttonhole filling
subtitle: Rows of buttonhole stitch worked into loops, not fabric, to build a raised mesh surface
excerpt: Detached buttonhole filling builds a self-supporting mesh of buttonhole stitches that sits above the fabric surface. After a foundation row fastened to the fabric, each subsequent row works into the loops of the previous row rather than entering the fabric, creating a lacy raised filling used in stumpwork and dimensional embroidery.
sourceNotes: Therese de Dillmont, Encyclopaedia of Needlework (1886), needle lace and detached filling entries. Caulfeild and Saward, Dictionary of Needlework (1882), detached buttonhole and needle lace entries.

content.text: Detached buttonhole filling belongs to the needle-lace family of stitches. A foundation row is worked into the fabric to create a line of loops along the top edge of the shape. Every subsequent row is worked entirely into the loops of the row above, with the needle entering loop rather than fabric. At the sides, the thread is couched to the fabric outline to hold the mesh in place. The finished mesh can be left open like lace, packed more tightly for a denser surface, or padded underneath for a raised stumpwork effect.

items.label: Thread
items.value: Stranded cotton, 1 or 2 strands for fine lace mesh; pearl cotton no. 12 for a firmer surface

items.label: Fabric
items.value: Firm linen or cotton in a hoop; the shape outline should be clearly drawn or padded

items.label: Needle
items.value: Tapestry needle size 26 or 28 for working into loops without splitting thread

items.label: Hoop
items.value: 15 cm hoop; keep fabric taut so the mesh tension is consistent

content.text: Secure a foundation thread along the top edge of the shape by couching or by making a row of small back stitches along the drawn line. This gives a firm base for the first row of buttonhole stitches.
Work the first row of close buttonhole stitches along the foundation thread, inserting the needle under the foundation thread each time rather than through the fabric. Keep loops even in size.

At the end of the row, take the thread down to the side edge of the shape and couch it to the fabric outline with a small stitch to hold the row in position. Then bring the thread back up to begin the return row.

For every subsequent row, work buttonhole stitches into the loops of the previous row only. Do not enter the fabric. Insert the tapestry needle under each loop from front to back, pass the thread under the needle tip, and pull through to form the new loop.
Couch the thread to the side edge at the end of each row, then return and work the next row into the loops just completed. Continue until the shape is filled.
On the final row, fasten the loops to the bottom edge of the shape with small couching stitches to complete the filled mesh.

attrs.heading: When detached buttonhole filling goes wrong

items.symptom: The mesh puckers or pulls away from the shape outline
items.cause: Side-edge couching stitches are missing or placed too loosely.
items.fix: Couch the thread firmly to the fabric outline at the end of every single row, not every second row.

items.symptom: Rows collapse into each other and the mesh loses structure
items.cause: The needle is splitting the loops of the previous row rather than passing cleanly under them.
items.fix: Use a tapestry needle. Its blunt tip slides under the loop without splitting it.

items.symptom: Loop sizes vary across the mesh, giving an uneven surface
items.cause: Thread tension changes from stitch to stitch.
items.fix: Draw each stitch through to the same tension. Keep a light, consistent pull and do not tighten loops beyond the size set in the foundation row.

items.symptom: Needle accidentally enters the fabric mid-mesh
items.cause: The needle angle dips too steeply and catches the fabric below the mesh.
items.fix: Hold the mesh away from the fabric with a fingertip while working each row to keep the needle working only into the loops above.

content.text: Detached buttonhole filling is the main filling stitch in raised stumpwork, where it covers padded shapes such as petals, leaves, and insects with a lacy surface that stands above the fabric.
